WHAT YOU CAN DO ABOUT
TUBERCULOSIS
The AJaska Tuberculosis Association is about to
begin its annual seal sale, an endeavor which has
always met with generous support from Alaskans.
Most people understand that the purpose to which
seal sale proceeds are put is a good one, but have
a hazy idea as to just what that purpose is and its
importance.
The National Tuberculosis Association, of which
the Alaska organization is a part, has been employed
in a relentless warfare against the tubercle bacillus
for about 35 years and has accomplished much. Prom
this long campaign physicians know now the most
vulnerable points to attack and the best weapons to
use. First in order of effectiveness is sanatorium
treatment. This outranks all other means of tuber
culosis control, as it furnishes the best means of
curing patients and at the same time removes sources
of infecfion from the community. Alaska is making
use of sanatoria to as large an extent as funds will
permit.
The number of institution beds utilized for the
treatment and segregation of cases of tuberculosis
is the best measure we have of the success of the
anti-tuberculosis activities carried on by public
health officials and voluntary agencies such as the
Tuberculosis Association. First on the list of objec
tives of the people behind the seal sale is the crea
tion of a demand for more sanatoria for the use of
citizens of such places as Alaska which do not have
enough beds to provide treatment promptly for all
patients who need it. Experience shows this re
quires at least two beds per annual death. Certain
States have already fulfilled this requirement; more,
including the Territory of Alaska, have made a good
start toward meeting the need; other regions have
done so littie that the effect is negligible.
Tuberculosis is a national problem, as the tuber
cle bacillus knows no boundary lines and the tuber
culous individual is more or less a nomad moving
about without restrictions, sowing the seeds of
disease while seeking health. It is a situation which
exists here and in all the States; it is a burden that
all should bear. By contributing to the seal cam
paign you can help.
Dr Henry D. Chadwick, new President of the
National Tuberculosis Association, has pledged his
organization to relentless warfare oh tuberculosis
throughout the coming year. Dr. Clifford E. Waller,
Assistant Surgeon General of the United States
Public Health Service, urges: The idea of eradicat
ing tuberculosis should pass from the realm of theory
into the sphere of practice. The program of finding
persons with tuberculosis must be intensive and wide
spread. It should cover the general population and
special consideration should be given to particular
groups such as age, sex, race, occupations and eco
nomic status, where the disease is more prevalent.”
In Alaska, tuberculosis is a great challenge. You
can do your part to help meet it when the Christmas
seals are distributed next week.
OUR STRENGTH IN THE AIR
Nothing could be a better guarantee of Ameri
ca’s peace and security than the announcement that
i two airplane plants in California alone now have
a capacity of 6,000 planes and motors per year. If
it is true that nine French aviators, flying nine
American planes, attacked 27 German Messerschmidts
and. "because of the superior maneuverability of the
American ships,” downed nine of the German craft
without losing one of their own, that, also, is a
guarantee of our peace and security.
Air strength lies in the potential capacity to
produce large numbers of good planes, not an array
of fabricated planes growng obsolete in their
hangars.
Isolated Finns
(Cleveland Plain Dealer)
Soviet-Finnish negotiations, now a month old,
are likely to achieve a place in the annals of diplomatic
failures along with the three-year disarmament con
ference at Geneva and the Anglo-Russian pourparlers
for an anti-aggression front. With the delegates re
turning to Finland after their third deadlock, nothing
but recriminations issue from Moscow.
There appear to be three insurmountable difficul
ties. The Finns are set against giving or leasing to
the Russians any territory for a naval base on the
mainland near Hagoe at the entrance of the Gulf of
Finland. They also reject the Soviet demand for a
frontier revision in the Russians' favor, the better to
protect the exposed city of Leningrad. To grant this
would be to court the fate of the Czechs, the Finns say.
It would mean abandoning their frontier fortifica
tions and leave the country exposed to invasion. The
Russians are also insisting on a territory in the Finnish
Arctic as a buffer belt to protect the port of Murmansk.
Along the southeastern border the Finns have
mobilized seven divisions of their small army. Pro
vocation. shout the Russians. The Finns' “unreason
able'’ attitude of insisting on defending their own
country, should the need arise, has greatly perturbed
the Kremlin.
The Finns find themselves Isolated. The Scandi
navian countries, Sweden and Norway, fear a Russian
attack on Finland. It would be looked upon as a first
step in challenging their own independence. There
fore, they had urged the Finns to make all possible
concessions. The Finns, certainly, could not expect
hope from Britain and France. Germany, while she
would like to control Finland and in the past lias made
repeated efforts to do so, would not act for fear of
compromising her delicate relationship with Moscow.
Since negotiations have broken down, the Russo-Fin
nish border becomes, for the present, more of a Euro
pean danger spot than the western front or the armed
frontier between the Third Reich and Belgium and
The Netherlands. I
Art in America

<New York Times)
One thing that must have impressed visitors to
the Masterpieces of Art exhibit at the World's Fair,
in addition to the wealth of beauty, was the number
of other visitors they found there. Though a special
admission charge of 50 cents was made to the art ex
hibit in addition to the admission to the Fair grounds,
it did not discourage crowds so large at times that it
was difficult for individuals to see the pictures. The
crowds were reminiscent of those milling around the
Van Gogh exhibit a few years ago and at the opening
of the Museum of Modem Art in this city. We ace
told that out in San Francisco the first few months'
gate receipts for the Art Masterpieces exhibit exceeded
those of the Sally Rand Nude Ranch. During the first
month 107,425 persons bought tickets for the art ex
hibit, or 30,000 more than those who paid to look at
Sally's young ladies.
These evidences of a greatly increased interest in
art in America are supplemented by those in the field
of publishing. Not only have a remarkable number
of art books been published this fall, but one of them,
"A Treasury of Art Masterpieces,” though priced at
$10, has had a first printing of 100,000 copies, and
stands at the top of some of the best-seller lists for
non-fiction books with sales that have already ex
ceeded 50,000 copies.
At a time when reactionary forces in so many
parts of the world seem to be turning back the clock
of civilization, these evidences of a great and rapidly
glowing interest in art in our own country are doubly
impressive.

By A. C. Gordon
1. Who was the American repre
sentative of the Colonies in Prance
during the Revotutlon?
2. What city is called "Gotham"?
3. If boiling water is kept boil
ing, how much hotter does it be
come?
4. In which Shakespearean play
does the character “Ophelia" ap
pear?
5. What English city is noted for
its cutlery?
ANSWERS

2. New York.
3. It does not get any hotter.
4. Hamlet.

MODERN
ETIQUETTE

By Roberta Lee
Q. If you have some extra fine
wine that you wish to serve at your
Thanksgiving or Christmas dinner,
should it be served as an appetizer
or with the dessert?
A. It would be preferable to serve
the wine with your after-dinner cof
fee, along with nuts and fruits.
Q. When a man invites another
man to luncheon or dinner, should
he order for both?
A. He should allow his guest to
give his order first, and directly to
the waiter. When dining with' a girl,
she gives her order to him and he
orders for both.
Q. Should the word “yours” fol
low such closes to a letter as “Sin
cerely," “Lovingly," and “Devot
edly”?
A. Yes. That is the preferred
form.

laws the most exact and determin
ate.”—Emerson.

proved that the President Is In line with

try and has outlined a policy which will

ular confidence In business, and lead to
a permanent prosperity.
The Secretary reviewed crop conditions
and other fundamental conditions
throughout the country, declaring that
all signs pointed to prosperous times. One
of the strongest Indications of business
expansion, he said, was the movement
among American manufacturers looking
to the enlargement of their export trade
Secretary Redfleld said:
"I am sure that the spirit of the Presi
dent's message read to Congress today
will strike a responsive chord In busi
ness circles all over the land. Already
such depression as had existed here and
there has begun to pass away. The
movement seems to be upward and for
ward generally. It is not a rush or a
boom, and It Is well that it is not. be
cause rushes and booms are apt to last
but a little while"

site speculation, debts are well liqui

competing power to the utmost. The cur
rency bill has removed .the threatened
danger from an. Inflexible' financial con
dition; the tariff, even by those who
oppose It, is admitted at the worst to be
much better than they feared, and at the
best, to be helpfuL What is there to

ant Secretary of the Navy. "AH we've

nese wall of defense around us we'tt

if that is our conception of defens-

F. D. Seeks New Grip
on U. S. Oil Industry
The Administration is planning to
seek congressional action this session
to re-establish the New Deal's power
to regulate the oil industry, wiped
out by the Supreme Court when it
held NRA unconstitutional and abol
•tshed the petroleum administrative
board.
Present plans call, it was learned
today, for President Roosevelt to
back the Thomas oil bill giving the
Government the right to regulate
production thru monthly state allo
cations.
The Government now has only the
Connally oil measure under which
the Federal tender board operates in
east Texas to control the flow of
"hot" oil.
Interior Secretary Ickes is a strong
supporter of the Thomas measure,
and recently said the decrease of
$700,000,000 to $800,000,000 in oil com
pany stocks occurred after Federal
control of the industry had been dis
solved.

Commerce Secretary. He will succeed
John Dickinson, recently transferred
to the Justice Department The
President also re-appointed Charles
H March as a member of the Federal
Trade Commission for a seven-year
term beginning Sept. 26.

Bank Dividend.
The United States Savings Bank
Monday will disburse among its
Stockholders of record March 20, a
Quarterly dividend of '7% per cent
the first quarterly payment on the
basis of 30 per cent annually. For
several years the bank has paid
egular dividends of 20 per cent and

United States Savings Bank the
largest dividend paying bank in the
District.
.Federal Reserve Digest.
A digest of rulings of the Federal
reserve board covering the year 1911
to 1923, has been issued by the
board. The digest is intended to
t present in accessible form the vari
ous rulings of the board and the
opinions of its counsel and related
matters and is expected to dispel
some of the confusion existing with
respect to Federal reserve board a<-
ti vi ties.
The digest lists and analyzes the
rulings of the Federal reserve board,
enumerates the various regulations
of the board and sets forth the Fed
eral reserve act and the various
Federal laws related thereto with
summaries and explanations of
amendments and the changes af
fected thereby. The digest is writ
ten in non technical language and
is intended to servo as a ref
erence for bankers and business
men, having dealings with the Fed
eral reserve system and to simplify
for them the roles and regulations
under which the system functions.

Commodity Market News.
By Cosmopolitan News Service.
NEW YORK, March 26. The
sharp break in wheat prices extend
ing over the past ten days, as a re
sult of which May wheat today is
at the lowest price level of the
season to date, has had a disturbing
effect on democratic flour trade.
Prices in the flour market are un
steady, despite assertions by milling
interests that good milling wheat
would not decline, and that the de
plorable situation In the feed market
has increased the cost of flour.
Buyers are unwilling to enter large
commitments, and the volume of
business is consequently small. Ex
port demand is also limited.
Since the promulgation of new
tariff rates, May wheat in Chicago
has broken 8% cents, while Winni
peg has declined 4% cents, making
a reduction in Chicago premiums
over Winnipeg of 4 cents a bushel.
Aside from the break in cotton,
irregular foreign exchange move
ments and the uncertainty expressed
in speculative circles concerning the
future of American business and in
dustry, there is nothing to account
for the decline in prices of wheat,
corn, and oats.
of interest is apparent In
principal provision, food, and feed
markets, with sellers anxious to
dispose of accumulating stocks, and
buyers inclined to hold off for lower
prices in hogs, lard, bran, rye, mid
dlings, hay and straw, oats, corn,
flour, barley goods, etc. There is a
falling off in demand for brewers’
stocks, hops and malting barley, the
bulk of the sales being for foreign
account.

'AUTO INDUSTRY
SETS HIGH
RECORD
More Than a Million Cars
Produced for First Quarter
of Present Year.
By MARSHALL B. WALKER.
Cosmopolitan News Service Staff
Correspondent.
DETROIT. Mich., March 26.
With a total output of around
1,100,000 cars, the first three months
of this year, the automotive indus
try now has swung into the closing
week of the first quarter with a
new high record established. Pro
duction so far has exceeded the cor
responding period of 1923 by ap
proximately one-third, It Is esti
mated, and March figures will ex-'
ceed those of January and Feb
ruary.
Usually the spring months are
the greatest periods of production,
but there are those who doubt if
this will be the case this year.
Early price changes undoubtedly
have had their effect and it is not
to be wondered at that questions
have been asked as to whether this
will reduce the normal proportion
ate increase in sales during the
coming months.
Caution Shown.
Production in some plants is run
ning only about parallel with sales,
it is true, and some d'ealers are
showing more caution than pre
viously so as not to overload. On
the other hand, many manufactur
ers still are increasing production
and other dealers are providing
against the spring demand.
Here are the fact in the Industry
today which are no’hing if not op
timistic.
Ford and Chevrolet are continu
ing their old pace of high produc
tion Willys-Overland is showing
constant gains and Dodge and
Hudson-Essex still are behind on
orders. Olds has Increased its force
of workmen and Paige-Detroit de
liveries have reduced the company’s
stock of stored cars nearly fifty
per cent.
Olds’ shipments so far this year
are more than four times the cor
responding period of 1923. Willys-
Overland is making 1,200 cars a day
and expects to set a March record.
April orders already on hand call
for 20,000.
General Motor dealers took twenty
more cafrs this first quarter than in
the corresponding period of 1923,
and. stocking up against the spring
demand, have more cars on hand
than at this time last year.
Durant plans to increase produc
tion to 10,000 cars in April, a gain
of about 3,000 cars over March.
May schedule calls for 110,000.
Make New Records.
Moon and Rickenbacker estab
lished new production records last
week and the latter company ex
pects to go still higher and reach
the peak of output next month.
Reports from the Franklin factory
state that March shipments have
been ahead of February and still
the unfilled orders have increased.
Optimism is expressed at the Ford
factory.
“In spite of the fact that the
weather has been against the rapid
delivery of cars, we feel opti
mistic,” says an official. “Our stocks
of cars showed a reduction March
1, and the rate of reduction is stead
ily increasing. We expect to have
delivered 200,000 cars by the end
of March."

Despite the heavy war
clouds over the Middle East
and the rambunctious atti
tude of the Russians in their
relations with the free world,
some Informed quarters in
Washington are disinclined
to believe in the possibility
of an armed clash because
of command troubles within
the USSR
Some American diplomatic
and political observers con
tend that ever since Stalin's
death the Communist leader
ship has never been firmly in
anybody’s hands. There have
been continual wrangles for
power with one man at the
top one day and another the
next.
The purges of V. M. Molo
tov and Dmitri Bhepllov were
not of the Stalin type. They
were not shot in the back of
their heads as was customary
in the past. They were given
insignificant jobs far away
from Moscow. This was not
done because Nikita Khru
shchev has a more tender
heart than Josef Stalin had.
but because he doea not com
mand the same power* with
the active supporters of the
regime as did the deceased
leader.
There is no question that,
given a chance. Khrushchev
would be at least as ruthless
as his predecessor. But. ac
cording to the American ob
servers, he does not have it.
For more than a year it was
common belief Inside and
outside the USSR that Kru
shchev had to rely on Georgl
Zhukov to maintain himself
ih power. Marshal Zhukov
was the Idol of the army and
had behind him all the men
in military uniforms. This
was a fair appraisal of the
situation in the Soviet Union
until his forced separation

missal caused no ripple
among the Soviet combat

diplomatic observers, some of
whom have been in the USSR
recently, believe the strug
gle for power In that in
trigue-ridden country Is only
In Its infancy and is likely to
develop until a really strong
man appears. They maintain
that all the present leaders
and would-be leaders are too
old to establish themselves
firmly. None has Stalin's halo.
Neither do they have his self
reliance and Ivan-the-Ter
rible fierceness. Hence, until
a real man rides in on a white
horse (here will be troubles
In the Kremlin high com
mand.
Observers conclude that
because of the unsettled con
ditions the Russians may
continue to rattle the sabre
and attempt to provoke
fringe wars by proxy but will
not dare challenge overtly
the free nations, to whom
America has pledged her full
military backing.
High-ranking officials fti
the State Department, and
especially our top military
leaders, do not share this op
timistic appraisal. They be
lieve that Khrushchev, whom
they consider shrewd but not
intelligent, may want to emu
late Stalin in military glory
and unleash a war in order
to gain complete and final
control over the USSR.
Whatever convulsions may

there is no question that the
battle order of the Soviet
ground, air and naval

Rokosaovsky's Caucasian

Turkey and Iran) has been
considerably strengthened by
the addition of new divisions
provided with atomic can
non. The number of Jet
bombers in that area also has
been substantially increased,
according to the excellent
Turkish intelligence.
The Soviet surface navy in
the eastern Mediterranean,
consisting of a couple of cruis
ers and several destroyers, is
merely a flag-showing affair.
But there are more than two
dozen submarines based in
Albania, with easy access for
more in Yugoslavia and
Egypt. There is rush work in
the Syrian harbor of Latakia
to permit submarine bases
there. Since financially hard
pressed Syria does not pos
sess Ruch vessels, it is obvious

done for the benefit of the
Red navy, which is bearing all

Similarly the Red air and
naval forces have been con
siderably strengthened in the
Far East wheie Vladivostok
bay has become strictly for
bidden waters for all foreign
ships.
Nothing has been done by

to justify these drastic meas
ures. Despite the abrogation

armistice which forbade us
to provide the two American
divisions and the ROK army

firepower, nothing has been
done by Washington to take
advantage of that release.
Those responsible for the
defense of the United States
and the free world must as
sume that the present Soviet
leadership—possibly because
of the struggle for power
within the Kremlin—con
templates an explosion which
might give the Red leader
the halo necessary to make
his position absolutely secure.

SINCE BABY CAME.
Since Baby came in last mid-May
I have not seen a single play.
The newer books remain unread
A little life I've conned instead.
So full of heavenly lines, and sweet
From tbe silken head to rose-pink
feet.
Since Baby came with needs so great
My hats and frocks are out of date;
Her carriage, cot and garments small
Have swallowed up our little all;
But other things I gladly miss,
My baby's blossom face to kiss.
Since Baby came a look of home
Upon our tiny bouse has come;
Her toys are scattered here and there
Her little touch is everywhere;
And love is dearer, holier flame,
And brighter burns since Baby
came.
—London Chronicle

WORDS OF WISDOM
In a recent address delivered by
F A Vanderlip, president oi the New
York National City Bank, he gave
utterance to these words of wisdom:
"The particular men who happen
for the moment to be occupying offi
cial positions in Washington and else
where, and who are laying unbear
able hardships upon the proper devel
opment of business in the United
States .are not perhaps primarily to
blame. The blame lies back of them
in an ill informed and frequent un
fair state qf public opinion. We have
bad a period of magazines and politi
cal muckraking w'hich has brought
about a condition where business suc
cess is looked upon as a crime, where
the man who has demonstrated that
he can manage his business well is
excluded from public counsel, and
where no small part of our govern
ment affairs have been put into the
hands of men who would be incom
petent successfully to manage busi
ness affairs.
“It is idle to rail at the public rep
resentatives of one party or another,
or at one administration or another.
We have got to get back to all that
and create a sounder, a more intelli
gent, and a more honest public opin
ion. That will never be done by a
policy of silence on the part of those
who represent important business in
terests You and other business men
must wake up to the fact that you
have a public duty in the education
of public opinion, and so long as you
refrain from exercising it, you will
not only hinder the industrial and
commercial development of this
whole country, but you will very di
rectly permit your own business to
be misunderstood and to be made the
subject of unfair and uneconomic at
tack.”
THE BUSINESS OUTLOOK
As viewed by Henry Clews, the
general business outlook is more
promising this week. Supplies of mer
chandise of nearly all kinds, he finds
are unquestionably light because of
Jhe slowing down which recent ap
prehensions necessitated. With the
recovery of confidence and with the
promise of a good harvest, increased
activity is only a matter of a few
weeks. It must be remembered that
industrial production has been ab
normally restrained for several
months. The steel trade for instance
has been running for weeks on 60
per cent of capacity; largely because
of enforced railroad retrenchment
which cannot be indefinitely prolong
ed. The railroads will soon be com
pelled to enter the market more free
ly, and with the assurance of good
crops and better rates will undoubt
edly place some liberal equipment
orders. In fact it would cause no sur
prise if the steel industry were to
show one of its customary sharp re
bounds before the end of the current
year. In the textile trades there is
also a better feeling. Both cotton
goods and woolens are comparatively
scarce and exceedingly strong. In
terior distributors report a good de
mand for nearly all classes of fabrics.
Importations of foreign goods are
coming in more freely; but the per
centage of these compared with the
nation’s product as a whole is not
large enough to have any serious ef
fect. Nevertheless the new tariff has
a potential influence; inasmuch as
any advance in prices here w'ould in
vite a rapid increase in importations
under existing conditions. The crop
out look continues most gratifying
There was a slight drop during May
in the condition of wheat, but the
government report still indicates a
yield of about 900,000,000 bushels,
which is much the largest yield ever
recorded.

GREAT COFFEE PAPERS.
During tne year 1913 the United
States imported 852,529,498 pounds
of coffee, having an entry value of
nearly $105,000,000. To the average
reader this may not appear very
startling, but a little circulation will
bring to mind the significance of
these figures. One pouud of finely
ground coffee will make no less than
three gallons of a reasonably strong
beverage. Our 1913 imports there
fore made at least 2,557,500.000 gal
lons. A standard gallon contains 231
cubic inches, or, putting it a little
differently, would nil a cylindrical
coffee pot 7 Inches in diameter and
6 inches high. The coffee imported
in 1913 would therefore fill a cylinder
7 inches in diameter and 242,188 mil
es high. Could such a cylindey be
erected it Would be necessary to take
care not to build it in the direction
of the moon’s orbit around the earth,
for that satellite’s average distance
from our planet being but 238,850
miles, it might knock off from the
top of our extended coffee pot, some
3,338 miles. Were it flexible and
the base well anchored however, it
might topple over and wrap itself
nearly ten times around the earth
at the equator. All of which is men
tioned merely to show that we drink
some coffee in this country.
A natural coffee plant grows into
a tree 14 to 18 feet high, having a
long and slender trunk without limbs
on the lower part. The plant has
numerous thin roots growing deep
into the earth, and one central or tap
root going straight down and almost
as long as the tree is high. When
cultivated, however, the plant is gen
erally not allowed to grow beyond 6
feet in poor and 8 feet in rich soil,
in order to facilitate its cultivation
and the gathering of the crop.
Healthy coffee trees produce in the
axilla of each leaf from t 2 to 16
buds which in flowering have an ex
quisite perfume. These powers be
come dark and wither and fail off in
two or three days, leaving groups of
seeds on the small stems. These in
turn grow into the coffee berries
which closely resemble dark red
cherries. Each berry contains two
seeds growing face to face and these
are the coffee beans of commerce.
The plant flourishes best in well
watered regions, in a sub-tropical cli
mate at an elevation of 1,500 to 5,000
feet, and in a rich soil. All these
elements are found to perfection in
Brazil, especially in the four states
of Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro, Espirito
Santo, and Minas Geraes, whose com
bined areas cover about one eighth
of the vast domain of the Republic.
This section produces about four-fif
ths of the world's supply of coffee,
and from Brazil, the United States
gets two-thirds of its supplv.
TOO MUCH LEGISLATION
Business men engaged In export
trade complain of an unusual condi
tion. Almost the whole world is suf
fering from trade depression which
seems to spring from a common cause,
too much legislation of the kind that
unsettles business.
In England business has been de
pressed for several years by a series
of radical laws. Trade has become so
unsettled that a few months ago the
governors of the Bank of England,
for the first time in the history of
that institution, addressed a protest
to the government.
German trade has not recovered
from the staggering blow of a special
war tax of $250,000,000 which was
levied last year, no one knows why.
France and other countries are de
pressed by financial difficulties grow
ing out of the political troubles inci
dent to the Balkan war.
Brazil is going through a period of
liquidation and acute business depres
sion, paying the penalty for a wild ex
periment in legislation. The govern
ment tried to regulate the price of
coffee, so as to make the crop more
profitable to the planters. TUa
scheme of "valorization” or govern
ment regulation of the price has
proved a failure and a large stock of
coffee must be disposed of.
The root of the trouble iu Mexico
is that the country has broken down
under the burdens of the “cientifico”
system of legislation, the futile at
tempt of former President Diaz to
make the country prosperous by
schemes promoted bv the government.
Australia and New Zealand have their
own peculiar troubles, and even Cana
da has "growing pains" as a result of
too much government booming of the
nortu west.
In our own country we have had a
tremendous output of legislation in
the past year. A tariff system which
has stood for fifty years has been
overturned, the currency system has
been revolutionized, and congress is
working on a large grist of new laws
to regulate business.
We are paying the penalty with
more acute depression than appears
jin any other country. The railroads
are in distress through loss of reve
nue, and half the industries of the
country are running on short time,
leaving millions of people out of em
ployment.
President Cleveland forced through
congress two revolutionary measures
in a little more than a year, a money
law and the Wllson-Gorman tariff.
The business of the country was par
alyzed by the shock and did not re
cover until after Cleveland had re
tired from office.
President Wilson has forced through
congress a far more radical revision
of the tariff than was attempted
twenty years ago, and a money law
scarcely second in importance to the
Cleveland, measure of 1893. In Jan
uary trade seemed on the way to re
cover from these necessary surgical
operations, but the improvement did
not last, and the trade depression has
become more acute in the past few
months, in the face of prospects for
large crops.
The patient has had a relapse be
cause congress has proved a surgeon
who don’t know when to stop. The
instruments are being sharpened for
another series of operations on the
helpless business man, before be h'AS
bad time to get on his feet and re
cover his strength. Business is par
alyzed and millions of people are suf
fering the pinch of want in the
midst of plenty, because the fanatical
surgeons don’t know when to go home
and give nature and the nurses a
chance. —L. R. Ardrey.

ROOSEVELT ON WILSON
As Colonel Roosevelt is a contribu
ting editor of the Outlook, it is not
impossible that the editorial is a
forecast of the line of attack he will
pursue in his campaigning this year.
The editorial, which bears the title
“Why?” is in full as follows:
"Business is disorganized. New en
terprises are not begun; old enter
prises are curtailing their business;
willing workers are laid off; every
morning newspapers report the cry
of the unemployed; dividends are re
duced or passed altogether. The crops
are promising; conditions demand
prosperity. But business is not good;
prosperity is conspicuously absent.
"Why?
"Mexico does not want war; the
United States does not want war;
and yet we are in a state of restrain
ed war with Mexico. American prop
erty has been looted; scores of Amer
ican citizens have been killed. The
American flag has furnished no pro
tection; for protection Americans
have fled to the English and German
flags. The hostility of the Mexicans
to the United States is increased;
their respect for the courage and ef
ficiency of the United States is dim
inished. That our relations with Eng
land Germany and Spain are not more
seriously strained is due to their un
paralleled patience. That we are not
embroiled in actual warfare with Mex
ico is due to the kindly offices of our
South American neighbors. No one
wants war, and yet we are on the
edge of war.
"Why?”
"We have had the responsibilities
and duties of sovereinty thrust upon
us in the Philippines. We have fulfill
ed those responsibilities and perform
ed those duties with notable success.
We have subsituted law for anarchy,
and a domestic government partially
representative for a foreign govern
ment wholly despotic. We have sub
dued hostile tribes, made life and
property safe, banished epidemics, es
tablished a public school system, built
good roads, promoted commerce and
industry and furnished protection to
a helpless people from foreign ag
gression. It is now proposed to ack
nowledge ourselves unable to contin
ue that protection without aid, and
to invite Japan and Great Britain to
share with us in furnishing it; to
abandon the attempt to protect the
peaceful citizens from the ignorance
of the few, and to leave this people
unaided to struggle their way as best
they can from childhood to maturity.
"Why?
“The answer is simple. This dem
ocratic administration does not be
lieve in a strong government. It is
afraid of a strong government. it
fears that the strong government will
be a despotic government. It seeks
refuge from that peril in weakness.
"It confronts great industrial org
anizations. It does not believe in mak
ing the government strong enough to
regulate such organizations and eom
pell them to deal justly with the peo
ple. It therefore endeavors to disor
ganize these business organizations
and convert each one of them into
two or more competing rivals. Busi
ness is disorganized because it is the
avowed policy of the present Demo
cratic administration to disorganize
business.

"Mexico is torn by contending fac
tions, neither of which recognizes the
necessary conditions of peace or the
modern laws of war. This Democratic
administration does not believe in
maintaining a government strong
enough to say to both factions: The
j laws of war toward noncombatants
must and shall be obeyed. So it looks
lon appalled but inert while bandits
plunder and assassins murder. It will
persuade, but not enforce; it will in
termeddle, but not intervene.
"it looks across the ocean and sees
an island people under the protection
of tlie American flag, learning under
American tuition the lesson of self
government. But it does not believe
that the United States government is
or should be strong enough to protect
land instruct a people on the other
side of the globe. It believes that this
nation neither has nor ought to have
the power to complete the task which
it has begun. It therefore proposes
that the United States enter into one
of those entangling alliances with
foreign nations against which Wash
ington warned his countrymen, pay
for this alliance by disavowing the
right of the United States to control
the canal built by the money of the
United States through the territory
of the United States, and then pull
down the flag in the Philippines and
retire, with confession of our weak
ness, from our uncompleted undertak-1
ing.
It is sometimes said that it makes
little difference what men believe if
their characters are good. No one
questions the character of President
Wilson and his advisers. Their in
tentions are excellent; their spirit is
patriotic. But they believe that a
strong government is perilous to in
dividual liberty, that in weakness is
safety. It is this belief which has in
vited disaster at home, brought dis
honor in Mexico, and now summons
us to retreat from the Philippines.
Consistently applied, it would with
draw our flag from Hawaii and Porto
Rico, abandon our protectorate in
Cuba, and transform the Panama
Canal into an international highway,
owned, regulated and policed by an
international commission.
The American people have the op
portunity this fall to elect a House
of Representatives which believes in
a strong government—able to control
the great industrial organization at
home, able to protect persons and
property in Mexico, and able to carry
to a splendid consummation the na
tional work so splendidly commenced
in the Philippines. It is for them to
decide whether the policy which P.
fifteen months has brought us to the
present conditions, at home and
abroad, shall be continued or halted
now and in 1916 reversed.
The Outlook believes with Alex
ander Hamilton that "an energetic
government Is necessary to (he safe-1
ty of the Union."
!hristain Workers' Assembly
TWENTIETH ANNUAL SESSION BEING HELD IN OSKALOOSA.
SOME EXCELLENT ADDRESSES BEING
SC DELIVERED.
At the opening session of the Chris
tian Workers’ Assembly at the
Friends church last night Rev. E.
Howard Brown, of Earlham, preached
an able sermon on "The Claims of the
Church,” taking for his text Matt.
1C: IS, "And I also say unto thee, thou
are Peter, and upon this rock I will
build rny church, and the gates of hell
shall not prevail against it.”
Rev. Brown said: "When Jesus
made this statement he was talking
to His disciples. Peter had answered
Christ’s question as spokesman for
the group. His disciples ail under
stood Him to mean that the church
was built upon the great truth Just
uttered. Peter, neither at this time
nor at any other claimed to be the
foundation of the church, nor to pos
sess alone the keys of the Kingdom.
The first claim of Christ for the
church was its Divine origin. The
church has always had her foes.
False religions have confronted her;
human institutions, social, reform,
charitable and philanthropic in their
nature, have imitated her but none
have approached her. And the church
has triumphed when facing such
mighty minds as Voltair, Rousseau,
Gibbon, Shelly, Hume and Ingersoll.
The foes of today are ministers with
in the church who are seeking to
change the fundamental doctrines,
and even the very mission of the
church.
“The second claim Jesus made for
His church was that it was to be His
representative on earth. The busi
ness of the church has not been
changed. Her enemies would wreck
her on the sidetracks of Sociology,
Philanthropy, Culture, or some hea
thenish cult.
"The third claim for the church
lies in her message. Christ sent men
out to preach His gospel. The
church has power to do what Jesus
did, the authority to say what He
said, and to continue what He begun
till the whole wide world is evangel
ized. The message has not been
changed—men have not changed.
There is no brotherhood-of-mau, nor
fatherhood-of-God outside the new
birth. W-e cannot substitute a new
message or a new way to be saved.
God’s message to the church may be
a social message, but His message to
lost men is not a social message. It
is Christ, a savior from sin, sanctifi
cation, social service, missions, giv
ing, Christian charity—these are mes
sages for believers, not for lost men.
"The Quaker church holds the key
to all ciiurch federation or church
union. No union meeting is ever
held whether two or twenty churches
unite, but what they unite upon our
platform. Christ only! Essentials
only! The C. E.. the Y. M. C. A.,
the VV. C. T. U. and all ministerial as
sociations come to our platform. We
have led the world to put away slav
ery, to give woman her proper place
bota in church and state. We hold
the position tonight upon which the
Christ’s prayer may be answered and
the churches all become one..
"The church was never more suc
cessful and prosperous than today.
The future church will be what we
make it. The work is the Lord’s and
the power is His, but it is ours to
consecrate and apply ourselves to
the great task before us.”
Tonight at eight o’clock Rev. Frank
Dell, of New Providence, will give an
address on "Social Service."
Wednesday morning at 9 o’clock
the Assembly will open with devo
tional led by Florence Baker, of Hart
land. The subjects of the morning
will be: "The Church and her Or
ganizations,” Rev. J. C. Bowles, and
“Tlie Priesthood of Christ,” Rev. G.
E. Guille, of Chicago. In the after
noon th<? subject will be, "Tlie For
eigner at our Door,’ by Rev. Doan, of
Lynnville. At night an address on
"Present Day Evangelism,” by Rev.
Guille.
A cordial invitation is extended to
the public to attend any or all of these
sessions.
The twentieth annual session of the
Christian Workers’ Assembly of the
lowa Yearly Meeting of Friends is
progressing nicely, and is proving of
great interest to all present. A well
filled program which continues over
Friday evening, comprises addresses
and round tables on vital subjects
pertaining to the church and the gen
eral welfare of mankind. The special
evening addresses for the week in
clude "Social Service,” which was
given last evening; "Present Day
Evangelism,” to be given Wednesday
evening; on Thursday evening “The
Claims of the Ministry,” and on Fri
day the closing address on the
"Evangelization of the World.”
Rev. Frank W. Dell, of New Provi
dence, very ably and forcefully dis
cussed on Tuesday evening the ques
tion, “Social Service:’’ He first took
up the subject in its broader view,
the world in its relation to social ser
vice, and spoke of the things that
have brought the world in contact
with the great social question. He
discussed many phases and gave
specific illustrations where social
service is needed to correct the
wrongs imposed upon many fellow
men, aud finally Showed that the
church must take the lead in this
great work. He said in part:
U) The church must adopt as a
positive policy “the setting up of the
order of heaven upon earth." This
will involve an unceasing and earnest
political campaign against all exist
ing evils. She will have to proclaim
herself the uncompromising foe of
the drink traffic, social vice, hoarded
wealth, commercial rapacity, etc.
She must Insist upon remedial as
well as patlative legislation.
(2) She must use every effort to
see that existing legislation is en
forced.
(3) She must insist upon more
spiritual and moral Instruction In the
public schools. She should urge that
every teacher of our young people
should be of unblemished character
and untainted morals. She should
stand upon the platform of the "open
Bible” for the public school. She
must proclaim her own message of
light fearlessly and Intelligently.
(4) The spiritually and physically
needy in every community should be
the special objects of her compassion
and care. She must see to supply
their needs with a view of wiuuing
them to Christ.
(5), She must look to it that her
campaigns are replete with fact as
well as -sentiment. TWs is a scienti
fic age When afi appeal'to the feel
ings is nqt as effective as an appeal
to the reason. She must avoid the
zeul that is not according to knowl
edge.
(6) She must learn to regard suit
able recreation as part of the daily
bread of the young people of any
community. If there is none, she
must provide it. If the amusements
are of a wrong kind, she must sub
stitute those of a right kind.
(7) If there is no bond of fellow
ship in the community the church
must seek to unite people in the ac
complishment of some laudable enter
prise.
Whilst in no case should the church
neglect cases of individual need, her
chief effort must be concentrated
upon the removal of the causes from
which suffering and w’ant proceed.
The greatest social service ever
rendered to society was when Christ
took upon Himself the seed of Abra
ham. And the church can now ren
der no greater service to men than
by bringing them into touch with
Him who is still able to save. But
before she can do this she herself
must be in touch with those who need
saving. And there is no better way of
obtaining this touch than by render
ing physical aid to men in their hour
of need.
Tuesday’s Sessions.
Services during the day of Tuesday
were also full of great interest. The
general theme of the day was "The
Church and the Community," and
under this head, papers were present
ed by Rev. R. R. Newby, of Des
Moines, on "The Church and the Ru
ral Community.” This was followed
by a round table discussion, led by
Rev. Alvin Hoskins, of Richland.
An Important feature of the day
was the address of Rev. George E.
Guille, of the Moody Bible Institute,
Chicago, on "The Exaltation of
Christ.” These Bible talks by Dr.
Guille are full of profit and are veri
table heart feasts to all who hear
them.
In the afternoon “The Church and
the City Community” was presented
by Rev. George Deshler, of Pleasant
Plain, and was followed by a round
table discussion, led by Rev. Meade
A. Kelsey, of Oskaioosa. In this dis
cussion the fact was brought out that
only about one-half of the population
of Oskaioosa were among the church
attendants, the balance being practi
cally without church influences.
Thursday’s Program.
The program for tomorrow is as
follows:
9:00 a. m.—Devotional, James Ren
frew, loWa Falls.
9:80 a. m. —The Church and Her
Congregation.
Men and Women, Clark Brown.
Camming.
Round Table, Anna Smith, Honey
Creek.
11:00 a. m. —Bible Hour, Rev. Geo.
E. Guille; subject: “The Advocacy
of Christ.”
The Young People, Edith Smith,
Ackworth.
Round Table, Win. S. Kltch, Bear
Creek.
8:00 p. m.—Address, "The Claims
of the Ministry,” Samuel Haworth.

VHRY SUDDEN DEATH
Mrs. Burris Expires While Attend
ing Globe Picnic.
Mrs. Mary L. Burris, 806 east Sev
enth avenue, suddenly dropped dead
of apoplexy about two o’clock this
afternoon while in attendance at the
annual Globe Correspandents' picnic
on Penn campus. She was 58. years, It
months and 12 days of age. Mrs.
Burris had seemingly been in perfect
health during the day and the end
came without the slightest warning.
The body was immediately removed
to the Cheesman Funeral Home. The
deceased leaves a daughter Mrs. P. L.
Mathews Eddyville a son Clarence
Coffin Ottumwa, a brother in Calif
ornia, and two sisters. Funeral ar
rangements will be announced later.
Wooden Bridges Washed Out.
June floods in many parts of lowa,
especially in lowa's northern coun
ties, are making great progress wip
ing out the old wooden bridges. In
Saturday night's rain, Chickasaw lost
five good-sized bridges. Other coun
ties report even greater losses, it is
not the wooden bridge alone that is
going, for quite a number of improp
erly constructed concrete bridges have
gone down. Franklin county will
have quite a bill to pay as a result
of the old-fashioned method of build
ing concrete structures without pro
per engineering construction or sup
ervision.
$1,500 Raised to Improve Road.
One of the leading thoroughfares in
to Monticello has always been one of
the: poorest pieces -of -roadway in
Jop)es county. j-The Monticello Im
provement- club has raised by sub
scription the sum of 31,600 to pave
this road and with a little help from
the county it will be possible to make
the improvement. The help no doubt
will be forthcoming. The sum of sl,-
600 is a good deal to be raised for a
purpose of this kind in a city the
size of Monticello, but after the im
proveraent has been made it will be
found that money was never expended
to better advantage.

pent, have been killed within the lim
its of Montezuma.

door service," it was revealed

staff.

A BOLD
HOLD UP
Main Street the Scene of an At
tempted Robbery.
THUGS ARE FRIGHTENED AWAY
Before Securing Any Booty—Joe
Schneider of Jennings Has an Ex
citing Experience With Two Strong
Arm Men—One Is Caught by Offi
cer Donahue, But the Other Gets
Away.
One of the boldest holdups in the
criminal annals of the city occurred
on Main street last night about 11:30
o'clock. That it resulted disastrously
to the thugs was only due to the
fight put up by their intended vic
tim.
The holdup occurred on Main
street in front of Gus Heller's saloon
and the three men implicated in the
affair were recent arrivals from Jen
nings. having reached this city the
night before. Joe Schneider, the vic
tim of the outrage, and two others
named Taylor and Conners, had been
employed on the railroad construe-
tion work at that place, and having
quit work they came to this city to
spend their money.
Schneider was the most industrious
one of the trio and had accumulated
a small amount of money. The other
two-had spent their money as fast as
it was earned and for some time had
been living on the bounty of their
friend.
Last night the three men were in
tiie Strand saloon and, after buying a
tew drinks, they went out on the
street. Schneider was ahead of the
other two and was walking toward
the corner of Second street when,
without warning, he was struck a vio
lent blow on the back of the head.
At the same time one of the men
threw his arni around Schneider's
neck, in an effort to prevent him
from crying out. He was too late,
however, as Schneider succeeded in
arousing the neighborhood by his vo
ciferous outcries.
He was thrown heavily to the side
walk and brutally kicked in the head,
but he continued to fight and ere for
help.
His yells attracted the people in
the adjoining buildings and they
came pouring into the street. Offi
cer Donahue was the first to arrive
and seeing him approach the thugs
took to their heels. One of them
dashed into the Strand saloon with
the officer at his heels. Seeing he was
caught, the man made no further at
tempt to escape and was placed un
der arrest. The other man, Conners,
ran down the street and succeeded
in .making his escape.
Schneider has several bruises and
a badly swollen eye to show for his
exciting experience, but counts him
self lucky in escaping without losing
his money. The holdup was exceed
ingly bold and was probably prompted
by hunger. The job was a very poor
one and was evidently their first at
tempt in that line.

A WONDERFUL ESCAPE.
Terrible Experience of a Hunter
With an Indian Band.
One of the most remarkable instances
of the escape of a white man from the
Indians was that of John Colter, a fa
mous hunter and trapper. On the day
in question he and his companion were
surrounded by 600 savage warriors.
The companion was instantly killed,
and Colter was captured. His foes had
no intention of saving his life, how
ever. They wanted the sport of put
ting him to the torture or at least of
playing with him as a cat plays with a
mouse. The chief asked him if he
could run. He saifl, "Not much."
He was released and told to save his
life if he could.
Colter darted away at high speed,
and most of the 600 savages set off aft
er him. There was a plain before him
six miles wide, bounded on the far side
by a river fringed with trees. Colter
had always been famous as a runner,
and his practice now stood him in good
stead. He made straight across the
plain for the stream, and the yells of
his pursuers lent him wings. His foes
had removed every shred of clothing
from his body, and the plain was cov
ered with prickly pears, so that his un
protected feet were lacerated at every
stride.
Half way across the plain he glanced
back and saw that only a few Indians
were following him. Again he ran on
and soon realized that one of his pur
suers was nearing him. He redoubled
his efforts, and blood gushed from his
nostrils and flowed down over his
breast.
The fringe of trees was near, but a
hasty backward look showed him the
pursuing brave close upon him with
spear raised. Moved by a sudden im
pulse. Colter stopped, turned and faced
the savage with outstretched arms.
The Indian was so taken aback ai
this unexpected movement that he
stumbled and fell! This was Colter's
opportunity. He ran back, seized the
spear anil, pinning his antagonist to
the ground, ran on.
Other savages came on, fiercer than
before-at the deatli of their comrade,
but Colter reached the trees, plunged
into their midst and then into the rivet
and swam to a pile of driftwood that
had lodged. He dived beneath it and
stuck his head up between two logs
covered with smaller timbers and
brush.
The Indians came up and searched
for several hours, but failed to find
him. Again and again they walked
over the driftwood. Luckily they did
not fire it, as he feared they would
At last they went away. Then Coltei
swam out and fled through the forest.
Seven days he went on, living on
roots and berries, wdtb no clothing, un
til at last he reached a trading post on
tlie Bighorn river. He never fully re
covered from the effects of this terrible
experience.—Youth's Companion.

various kinds of playthings. Don't
eAer give a "bad" boy up. Give him
something to do.

DELMONICO NARROWLY ESCAPES
TOTAL DESTRUCTION.
CAUSEO BYBURNINC CREASE
Kitchen and Contents Go Up in Smoke
-Sad Results of Frying
.Oysters.
'om Saturday's Daily Gazette.
Temporarily the Delmonico restau
rant is out of commission and MIessrs.
Parque Co. will. be unable to do
business until extensive repairs shall
have been made to the place. A fire
that had its origin in the kitchen at
about 1:30 this morning is responsi
ble for it.
A number of customers were in the
place and the kitchen crew was busy
getting out orders. The cook was
engaged in frying some oysters. and
in some unaccountable manner the
grease in the trying pan caught fire'
and exploded' with the force of a
charge of powder, filling the room
with ai sheet of flames and smoke.
So great was the power exerted by
the explosion that it seemed to blow
the roof off and it Was miraculous
that none of the inmates were injur
ed. Fortunately they managed to
escape, and joined by the guests in
the dining room made a hasty exit
onto the street.
An alarm of fire was sounded and
the deparement responded promptly.
By the time of its arrival the interior
of the kitchen was a mass of fire and
flames which roared like a furnace
and it was with great difficulty that
the fire was prevented from spread
ing. By hard work i was confined to
the room in which it originated,, but
before it could be extinguished the
kitchen and pantry and all they con
tained were gutted, nothing being sav
ed.
For a time it seemed that the ad
joining buildings were also doomed
and the inmates of the Sideboard sa
loon hurriedly began to empty that
place of its furniture, stock and fix
tures. Their work, however, proved
to have been unnecessary, as the fire
did not eat its way through the di
viding wall and only a little smoke
found its way into the saloon.
The building to the east did not
fare quite so well. The ground floor
is occupied by Vale Potter and the
second story by the Neel apartment
house, The heat from the fire caused
one of the windows in the second
story to break and the contents of one
of the rooms were considerably dam
aged by smoke and flames.' No fur
ther injury was wrought.
Parque Co. carried no insurance
and cynsequently their loss is total.
Mr. Parque stated this morning that
he was not prepared to estimate the
amount of damage sustained by his
firm, but thought it would be between
$500 and $1,000. The building occu
pied by them is owned by H. H. Mund
of Denver and is covered by insur
ance.
As soon as the necessary repairs
can be made Parque Co. will re
sume business.

Wells, Nev., Jan. 9.-Additional de
tails were received here tontight re
garding the tragedy yesterday at the
Keystone mine of the New York
Nevada Copper Mining company,
when 12 union miners attacked Su
perintendent Traylor for the alleged
purpose of running him out of town,
and which atta.ck resulted in the
death and wounding of several of the
miners' party. Since a branch of
the W~stern Federation of Miners
was organized a few weeks ago on
the Ely with about 100 members
drawn from the various mines in the
district, the miners are, said to have
taken a decisive stand in labor mat
ters, the particular object of their
attack being the New York Nevada
company.
Superintendent John A. Traylor,
whose home is in Denver, and who
was formerly connected with the
Fernando Mining company of Du
rango, Mexico, and also the Union
Copper and Gold Hill mines of North
Carolina, had been notified on several
occasions that he had better leave
camp, presumably because he had or
dered 'a reduction in his employes'
wages. Telegrams were sent to New
York, it was said, threatening to flood
the mines and to take other. strong
measures unless the superintendent
was removed.
Ultimatum Is Delivered.
Yesterday morning a delegation of
three men, Bill Carothers, Frank
Wolf and M. Parker, called at Tray
lor's home at Ely and presented an
ultimatum to be signed and agreed to
within 12 hours. Traylor immediately
took ar buggy and started' for the
mines, a few miles west of Ely. On
a(riving at Lane City,four miles away,
he was halted by a mob of miners
who, after some talk, allowed him to
proceed. Traylor then proceeded to
Keystone, where a smelte. 'nd con
centrator is being erected, L.1 tele
phoned from the company's office to,
Sheriff G. F. Newman and District
Attorney Walker, ask'3ng protection.
President Lloyd of the miners' un
ion, it is charged, sent a committee
of miners into the office to order Tray
lor to come out and surrender, finally
going in himself and directing mat
ters. Traylor talked with Lloyd for
some time, calling attention to the
fact that the 12 hours allowed in the
ultimatum had not expired. Lloyd
said that had nothing to do with the
case, that he had another matter to
settle, and that Traylor must sign
a new scale of wages at once. The
commitee then asked him to go along
quietly or they would be compelled
to take him dead or alive. Johnson,
one of the miners' committee, re
marked that they expected trouble,
but was ready for it.
Then the Shooting Began.
Traylor endeavored ·to argue with
the men, it is said, but Lloyd ordered
his companions to seize the superin
tendent and bring him along. Ten of
the men started for Traylor, who
grabbed a gun aid began shooting.
At the first shot the miners made
a dash for the do6r. The men that
were shot were those who had grab
bed Traylor and were trying to over
p'ower him. Their names are Janies
Staggs, Sam Johnson and J. Smith.
The names of the three wounded men
are not given.
After the shooting Traylor went to
Ely by a roundabout route, the main
road down the canyon in the vicinity
of Lane City being patrolled by arm
ed strikers. On his arriva;, at Ely,
Traylor surrendered to Sheriff New
man.

Why Kill Our Children
By Dr. Donald A. Dukelow,
Secretary Public Health Education Section of the
American Public Health Association
are considered the leading cause of death by Dr.
Frank Dickinson of the American Medical Association. He
has invented a new measure of society’s lose from death. Instead
of considering a death to be the loss of one life, he considers it
to be the loss of a number of years of living, or a number of years
of production, during which the person who died might have
made a significant contribution to society. If we measure the loss
of life in terms of working years lost, that is the years between
the ages of 20 and 65, we find accidents cause a greater loss to
society than even heart disease. If we consider life years lost in
terms of unfulfilled epectation of life at the time^of death, acci
dents are ^second only to heart disease. This is because many of
the accidents take the lives of younger people who would have
had many years of living and many years of production if their
life had not been terminated by an accident. It is surprising that
we spend so little time in learning how to prevent the Occidents
that cost us ao many unlived years.
Accidents are very expensive. Dr. Louis I. Dublin has cal
culated that a family must spend approximately three times its
annual income to raise a child to maturity. That means that the
average High School youngster has cost his parents a cash out
lay of $15,000 more or less, to say nothing of the taxes that they
paid for the maintenance of the schools he attends, the parks in
which he plays, the libraries that contribute to his understanding,
and the police that give him protection. If you had a cherished
heirloom in your home, worth $15,000, you most certainly would
protect and care for it and, try to guard it from injury. Yet you
permit this valuable youngster of yours to drive the family car
with a minimum of instruction, or you let him have a motor
scooter which affords him much less protection than the car. You
encourage him to do jobs around the house without instruction on
a safe way to do them and otherwise expose him to unnecessary
danger without taking the trouble lo develop the safety minded
ness that is his best protection.
Let’s consider a slightly older group of people. Let us con
sider those of full maturity who have established a home in which
they have one or more children, and where the head of the house
hold has a responsible job that is supporting this family and con
tributing to the needs of society. Children who have not been
trained in safety, grow up to be adults who do not understand
the danger of the world in which they live. Industrial safety codes
protect the worker on the job, but for some reason or other the
safety trained worker fails to carry ovgr into his home the prin
ciples of safety learned at the factory. The man who would re
fuse to work at an unguarded machine will operate power tools in
his basement, with no safe guards whatsoever: will attempt to do
his own electric wiring, will fail to keep the ice off his back steps,
will use make-shift ladders and will forget to install all of the
safety devices that his home should have for the protection, not
only of himself, but the rest of his family. That is one of the fac
tors that makes home accidents outnumber even highway acci
dents. This home is also the place where older people spend most
at their time. When Grandma gets to the place where her vision
is poor and her reaction time is low, she is likely to have an ac
cident under situations that a younger person could handle with
out much difficulty.
But let’s get back to the consideration of children. The chief
cause of death of young people from ages one to 19 is accidents.
The predominance of accidents as the cause of death and their
great prominence as the cause of permanent disability, has lead
to a national child safety movement which has been gaining mo
mentum over the years, but this year has crystalized into a uni
ted effort to save the live* of children. The National Safety Coun
cil, and the Toledo Safety Council, a Red Feather service, are at
tempting a broad program of education to protect our children
from unnecessary death and disability. This program has too
many interests to describe them *11, but few might illustrate
the point we are discussing.
Most schools that transport children by bus has a safety pa
trol of school children on the bus to maintain order and protect
the children from accidents. And in most High School there is a
safety program going on in the school itself in which a group with
special interest in accident prevention patrol the halls and stairs,
search the school for accident hazards and otherwise protect their
fellow students from unexpected danger. Much of this safety edu
cation in the schools could be carried over into the home if pa
rents would only give their children a free hand. Too frequently
a child who has learned a safety concept at school receives such a
cool reception at home when he suggests an improvement in his
home, that he. soon is discouraged and fails to bring home the
safety ideas that could improve the conditions under which he
lives.
Just what are the principle hazards causing accidental death
in young people from birth to 19? Top on the list are motor ve
hicle accidents, drowning, bums and conflagrations follow in
order mentioned. What can we do, as parents, to reduce the an
nual toll of childfen lost through accidents? To get to this answer,
we will have to consider the major hazards in each age group.
In the group under 5 years of age, mechanical suffocation is a
leading accidental cause of death in Ohio. This is most frequent in
infants less than a year old. It is the kind of thing you read
about in the newspaper where a child *is found dead in bed, or
goes into a choking spell from which he does not recover. A small
portion of suffocation accidents come from giving very small
babies soft pillows in which the face may become buried, or
tying them into bed with one of those fancy straight jacket af
fairs that chokes them when they attempt to turn over. The great
majority, however, are due to a swelling of the mucous mem
branes of the nose and throat when the child has a cold. The
speed with which obstruction of the breathing apparatus can oc
cur is surprising and alarming. Very young infants, with a cold
or other nose and throat infection should be carefully watched
throughout their illness as insurance against this type of acci
dental death. Automobile accidents are the second cause of death
in this group under five. Nearly two-thirds of them result from
the child as a pedestrian, being hit by an automobile. In the bal
ance of them the child is a rider in an automobile at the time he
suffers his accident. It is possible to teach youngsters the dangers
of running into the street, a well as how to cross streets when
running errands, or going to call on their playmates. It is signifi
cant that most automobile accidents involving small children, in
volve a child who is on foot and has gotten in front of a moving
automobile.in

With the school age group from 5 to 14, the picture shifts.
The most frequent causes of death are accidents involving motor
vehicles, with accidents in which the child is the pedestrian pre
dominating. Drowning becomes second in importance, and burns,
conflagrations and explosions next. In this age group accidents in
public places become much more important than in the younger
group, while accidents in the home decrease. Preventive measures
are much the same.
I think you can see from our discussion of causes of acci

THAT CHURCH MEMBERSHIP
Where is it? In some little country
or village church which you left
behind when you moved to town,
but which you fondly think of as
the “old home church" church? Or
is your membership just a "scrap
of paper,” which you keep in
desk or trunk? Or is it in the church
where you live and which you are sup
posed to attend and work in?
For various reasons not a few once
active church members on removing to
town or some other country com
munity, leave their church member
ship in the “old home" church. Some
give sentimental reasons—“So many
tender personal ties;” “So many hal
lowed family associations;" "I just
can't give up mother's old church”;
“All my people are buried in the old
graveyard there, and there I expect
to be buried.” Some justify them
selves by financial considerations—
"The ‘old home’ church is weak and
needs the little 1 can give, and they
don’t need me in town"; "I am afraid
if 1 quit paying there, the old church
will go down"; “If 1 move to the town
church, they’ll assess me too high."
And so for these and other reasons
there are enough ‘‘grave yard" and
“old ehureh" and “trunk” membership
Methodists living under the shadow of
our eity and town and mill village
churches to almost double the mem
bership of these churches, or organize
another church, if they would only
move their membership. And move
it they ought. Not one of the excuses
given will bear examination. If the
five dollars they pay to the "old
home” church is all that keeps the
breath in it. it is certain that such a
ehureh can no longer be useful. It is
as false sentiment as it is poor religion
to belong to a “grave yard" rather
than a living church at your door. It
is certain that you will not regularly
attend or actively work in the town
church to the support of which you do
not contribute anything, and by not
actively identifying yourself with it,
you are shipwrecking the religious in
terests of yourself and your children.
This is a false sort of loyalty to moth
er’s “old church.” The time to move
your membership is now at the begin
ning of the new conference year, be
fore any assessment is made and they
begin to count on you at the other
place. And it is almost inconceivable
that the pastor of the “old home"
church would jeopardize the highest
spiritual interests of any family and
sacrifice the interest of the church as
a whole by trying to persuade people
to “hold on with the old church anoth
er year,” though they do say it is
often done.

One of the most important tables
ever compiled by the Interstate Com
merce Commission has been supplied
by Secretary Moseley to Senator Tip
man, who procured its printing as a
public document. It is a list of colli
sions and derailments where the em
ployes had been on duty an excessive
number .of hours and a list of personal
injuries to employes due to having
been at work excessively long.
These are railroad reports and not
the results of investigations by the
commission, and they do not include
personal injuries that bad no obvious
connection with the condition of the
employe. The facts disclosed by this
tabulation are startling.
Eight railroad men were killed and
thirteen injured as the result of acci
dents caused by overwork. In one case
a man who had been on duty thirty
two hours was sent out flagging and
went to sleep on the track. In nine
other cases in this list of personal in
juries men had been at work continu
ously for twenty hours or more.
In collisions and derailments due ta
lack of sleep or exceptional fatigue
thirty-five persons were killed and 147
injured. In one case the man had been
at work forty-eight hours. In nine cases
men had been at work twenty-four
hours or more—one was forty-seven
and a half hours at work and another
was thirty-eight—and in several other
instances men had been at work more
than twenty hours.—Philadelphia Ree
ord.

No important developments appear tc

Which sustains confidence in the business

more evident in production and distribu

orably with a year ago, and road sales
men obtain orders making a substantia
aggregate in the principal staples.

values have advanced to the highest aver

isfactory and money works easier, while

NEW YORK.
Cross currents in trade and crop con
ditions prevent generalization. There has
been a further slight improvement in
crop condition. This has made for a
more optimistic feeling as to ultimate
yields and future trade in the sections
enjoying even a small share of seasonable
weather, but the great majority of cities
and particularly those in the eastern half
of the country complain of continued slow
retail trade and collections. On the other
hand the reports as to fall trade are quite
satisfactory, a reflection possibly of the
fact that retail stocks of heavy goods
were well cleaned up last winter. Crop
uncertainties and the fact that reorder
business this spring has been practically
absent in many lines, however, induce
conservatism as to future ordering and
there is less disposition to embark freely
in future commitments until the situa
tion becomes clearer.

Monterrey To Restore Historic Bishop’s Palace
PLANS MADE
FOR MORE
PARKS
—_—
MONTERRE( Julv 13-On Mon-|
day afternocn “he Mexican govern
ment _officially turned over to the
Monterrey Sub-Coramittee of the
National Tourist Debartment, Mon
terrey’s historic old landmark, the
Bishop's Palace. This simple act, at-
tended by state and city officials and
members of the Tourist Sub-Com-
mittee, made it a fact at last. after|
years of planning and of delays and
difficulties, that the Obispado will be
restored, the road leading to it pave
ed, and the desolate hillside where ti
stood in dignified ruination for so
long, made a garden-spot and a cul-
tural ceinter.
The following listened to the read-
ing of the act by Ing. Jose Muguerza,
Head of Monterrey's Sub-Committee
of the Tourist Department; Sr. Fran
cisco E. Velasco., representing the
Federal Government: Sr. Jesus M.i
Baez, representing the State govern-
ment of Nuevo Leon: Sr. Antonio
Malo, Secretary of the Sub-Cnmmit-l
tee of the Tourist Department; Sr.
Roberto Garza Sada. President of
the Committee for the Preservation
of Natural Beauties and Na!ionall
'Monum>nts; and Dr. Amado Fer
nandez, who will be in charge of the
Obispado Museum, being well-known
as an authority on Monterrey his
toriana, and devoted to the preser
wvation of relics, art objects, and his
torical data.
The Obispado will be turned over
for ma minimum ow twenty years to 1
the Tourist Committee, which plans
during that time to make the museum
and old building so much a pride of
the city and nation that it will not
be taken from the control of Mon-
terrey people ever again.
Already, having waited patiently
for the actually celebration of theJ
act of turning over the Obispado,
historical collections for its museum
have been made. Among the objects i
also turned over to the Tourist Com
mittee for the museum are several
old carved doors of wood, a number
of historical worked-iron window
bars and gates, a baptismal font, sev
eral old lanterns, flags from the
epoch of “Emperor” Iturbide, two
old cannons and other objects.
The first thing done will be to
make the building strong and safe,
repairing some weaknesses in floors
and walls; then it will be restored, as
much as possible, to its originnal ap-
pearance and plan. The road will be
paved which leads to it, and gardens
will be put in.
The Obispado, dominating the city
from a hill to the south, was built in
1788 by Bishop Verger.

Chamber of Commerce a day or so

set for this week at the latest. He
may continue on to Mexico City after
his flight here.

Fleet Of 100
Private Planes
To Fly Here
v
The list airplane excursion to Mon-
Iterrey from Stinson Field San An-
Itnnio. which occurred some months
ago, having proved so successmul and
so popular, a second and more elab
orate tour-by-air of Mexico is plan
ned, which will get under wav in
the middle of October. The tour,
under the direction of Mrs. Harmon,
an expert aviatrix and wife of the
manager of Stinson Field, will con
sist of about one hundred airplanes,
of all types, and sizes, and carrying
capacity, fifty having already sign
ed up, well in advance of the final
startin gdate.
The planes will make their tour as
follows: First flight, San, Antonio
direct to Monterrey. Stop of one day
in Monterrey. Flight to San Luis
Potosi. Stop of one day in San Luis
Potosi. Flight to Mexico City. Sev
eral days stopover. Return flights,
Mexico to Tampico, Tampico to
Brownsville, Brownsville to San An
tonio.
The Federal Department of Com
munications will send an expert
aviator from the army with an es
cort, to guide the expedition over
Mexicos mountains, and to accom
pany the mon the return trip as
well.
Many special courtesies and festiv
ities are being planned for the air
minded tourists in each of the cities
at which they plan to land.
New Building To
Be Inaugurated
The beautiful new building of the
Bznco Credito Industrial and ‘Ja
Nacional” Insurance Company, erect
ed by “La Nacional” at a cost of
250,000 pesos will be formally in
augurated on next Monday, the 22nd
of this month. Handsomely modern
i without being extreme in design, the
‘new building will be air-conditioned
throughout ,and equipped with every
scientific device for comfort and ef
ficiency. State, city, and govern
‘ment officials, besides many leading
business men, have received invita
tions to attend the inauguration,
which will be held at 9:30 P. M. The
first floor will be cocupied by the
Credito Industrial Bank; the second
floor by the “La Nacional” offices.
Other floors will be rented.
Fire At
North Market
A fire, which broke out at 5 o'clock
in the morning, destroyed the lower
floor of the big North Market last
week, despite valiant efforts of the
fire department, which arrived speed
ily, but was handicapped by poor
equipment. equipment at pre
sent in process of purchase. The
damage to the market itself, not
counting what various stall owners
lost in merchandise, is estimated at
10,000 pesos at least.

Construction Of
Crematory Oven
Again the question of a crematory
oven for garbage and waste is be
fore the city, with evidence this
time that practical results may come
of discussions, since city, and state
lofﬁcials. and the Coordinated Health
iServices of the Federal Government
may each pay a third of the costs,
thus bringing the economics of the
oven within reasonable perspective.
It is estimated that such an oven
would cost $30,000 pesos. The deter:
mination to rid the city of the dang
er of garbage-dumping in the dry
river-bed has reached proportions in
which the three agencies have agreed
|to cooperate, for ridding the city of
'such dumping would undoubtedly
bring down the percentage of fly
carried and rat-carried diseases, these
having been brought to public at
tention by the Health Departments
with renewed vigor this summer,

and making other concrete prepara

plan to get children out of city

has been given offices in the Muni
cipal Building. Anyone with ~sug
gestions, help, contributions for
equipment, or other business or aid
to offer, may locate officers of the
committee there.
Train Accident
Being Investigated
Investigations as to the cause of
the accident which resulted in two
ceaths and a numger of persons
wounded when two trains on the
Monterrey-Laredo line crashed last
week, are being conducted. So far,
no official reason for the accident,
which completely destroyed two
coaches, has been given out. The
dead, and the greater part of those
Lurt, were railway employees,

be seriously damaged, engineers ad

age it, it may be easily repaired at
